I have always believed that the sea remembers everything we are too careless to hold. It takes our footprints in the morning and smooths them away before we return at noon. It takes bottles and bones and broken boats and turns them over for centuries in darkness. When I was a child, I thought the tide was breathing, and in a way I was right.

My grandfather would take me to the rocks before anyone else in the house was awake. He carried a chipped enamel mug of tea and wore the same blue sweater every season. He did not talk much on those walks, which taught me that silence can be generous. We crouched beside tide pools and waited until still water revealed itself as a busy city. There were crabs no larger than coins, sidling beneath shadows with an ancient embarrassment. There were anemones that closed around my fingertip, startlingly strong for something so soft. My grandfather named nothing for me unless I first tried to describe what I saw. Not the red one, he would say, but how does it move when it thinks nobody watches? That question has followed me into every classroom, office, friendship, and grief I have known since. How does a thing move when it thinks nobody is watching, including, perhaps, myself?

Later, we moved inland for my father's work, and the horizon became fields and motorways. I learned to love rivers, but rivers always seem to be going somewhere with purpose. The sea, by contrast, arrives and departs without ever seeming to leave at all. As a teenager, I found that contradiction unbearable, because I wanted every feeling to resolve. I wanted heartbreak to become wisdom quickly, and confusion to become a plan by September. Nothing in my life obliged, least of all the people I loved and tried to keep still.

My mother kept gardens she could not control and loved them for exactly that reason. She planted sweet peas along fences and forgave them annually for choosing their own direction. She kept letters from friends she had not seen in twenty years, tied with kitchen string. When I asked why she saved them, she said some people live on in handwriting. At the time, I rolled my eyes, because youth often mistakes tenderness for mere clutter. Now my own drawers contain ticket stubs, stones, postcards, and one inexplicably treasured rusty key. I do not know what lock it opened, which is perhaps why I cannot throw it away. Some objects are useful because they hold a door closed; others matter because they remain open.

In my twenties, I worked in a bookshop that smelled of paper dust and winter coats. People came in asking for books they described only by the color of their covers. A woman once wanted the sad green one her sister read during a summer in hospital. We found it together after an hour, and she held it like a recovered photograph. That job taught me that memory is rarely organized by author, title, or any sensible system. We remember the weather around a book, who lent it, and what our lives were refusing then. We remember meals by arguments, cities by staircases, and years by songs we can no longer hear casually. A friend of mine can date almost any photograph by remembering what shoes he owned. Another knows her life entirely through houses: the blue kitchen, the damp flat, the attic room.

I think I measure mine in bodies of water, real and otherwise. There was the quarry lake where we swam despite signs, thrillingly certain of our invincibility. There was the canal in Amsterdam where I cried after a phone call and pretended it was rain. There was the hospital sink where I washed my hands after my daughter was born, shaking. Water was there at the beginning again, absurdly ordinary and completely insufficient for the moment. She arrived with a furious face and a grip that immediately recalled those tide pool anemones. I understood then that beginnings rarely feel clean; they feel wet, loud, and alarmingly alive.

Now she is old enough to ask why waves do not stop and where the moon sleeps. I try to answer honestly without turning every mystery into a lecture she must endure. I say the moon is awake somewhere else, visiting other children with other questions. She accepts this in the practical way children accept both facts and stories as weather.

Last summer, I took her to the same rocks my grandfather once showed me. The blue sweater is gone, and the enamel mug lives, chipped further, on my kitchen shelf. She crouched beside a pool and whispered that we needed to be patient for the city. I had not told her that phrase, or if I had, I did not remember doing so. Perhaps some sentences pass between generations the way seeds travel, unnoticed, on a coat sleeve. A crab emerged, considered us with an indifference perfected over millions of years, and continued sideways. She laughed and said it was dancing badly on purpose, which would have delighted my grandfather.

In that moment, I felt time behave less like a line and more like a tide pool. Everything past was not behind us; it was simply hidden for a while under still water. Grief, I have learned, does not shrink so much as teach us larger rooms to keep it in. Joy does something similar, expanding cupboards we thought were already full of ordinary days. I no longer expect the sea to give me answers arranged in any useful order. I go because it reminds me that returning is not the same as repeating. Each wave is both an arrival and a farewell, and somehow neither cancels the other. Perhaps a life is not something we solve, but something we learn to watch with patience. Perhaps we are all small cities under still water, waiting for someone kind enough to crouch down.
